title: Will AI reduce your work? It adds work: managing it. · hancrafted
description: Why AI adds work rather than removing it, and the management skills that let you take on far more complex tasks with it: hand off work with enough context, onboard a new team member like a new AI session, and break a complex project into chunks with clear seams between them.

slides.text: Will AI reduce your work? It adds work: managing it. From execution to management The work does not shrink. It changes, and you move up.

Every revolution, one card A cheaper unit does not mean less total work Jevons argued Watt's inventions economised heat and that further improvement would accelerate coal use; separately, in Scotland coal per ton of iron fell to under a third while total consumption rose about tenfold 1 . Sources (1) Jevons, The Coal Question (1865) ( opens in a new tab ) econlib.org The tool lifts the tasks left to people When ATMs quadrupled, tellers per branch fell by more than a third, yet branches rose by more than 40 percent and tellers moved towards relationship banking 1 . Sources (1) Autor, Why Are There Still So Many Jobs? The History and Future of Workplace Automation ( opens in a new tab ) aeaweb.org The plough is the weaker card Boserup finds the plough often prevented a fall in output per man-hour rather than raised it, and the extra work came from cropping land more often 1 . Sources (1) Boserup, The Conditions of Agricultural Growth ( opens in a new tab ) biw.kuleuven.be Some workers did rise, by several routes A contemporary defender of the factory system claimed regular, skilled workers could advance to overlooker, manager or partner, and 18 percent of a sample of British mechanics and engineers became hired engineers and managers; but owners found managers by many routes, and no source measures how many came from the shop floor 1 2 . Sources (2) Ure, The Philosophy of Manufactures (1835) ( opens in a new tab ) archive.org Meisenzahl and Mokyr, The Rate and Direction of Invention in the British Industrial Revolution: Incentives and Institutions ( opens in a new tab ) nber.org Steam shifted a region's skill mix English counties that used more steam engines had a larger share of skilled workers; no study found follows individual adopters rising, and schooling and wage evidence for the period is mixed 1 . Sources (1) de Pleijt, Nuvolari and Weisdorf, Human Capital Formation During the First Industrial Revolution: Evidence from the use of Steam Engines ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org AI completes longer tasks on its own The task length a frontier model completes at 50 percent success was about 50 minutes in early 2025 and has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019 1 . Sources (1) Kwa et al., Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (METR) ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The gain is real but conditional 758 BCG consultants using AI finished 12.2 percent more tasks, 25.1 percent faster, at over 40 percent higher quality inside the model's frontier, and were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct on a task outside it; a trial with 16 experienced developers found a 19 percent slowdown with early-2025 tools 1 2 . Sources (2) Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper 24-013 (SSRN 4573321) ( opens in a new tab ) mitsloan.mit.edu Becker, Rush, Barnes, Rein, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The same prompt can answer differently Across five models and eight tasks run ten times with settings meant to be deterministic, accuracy varied by up to 15 percent between runs, unlike a plough or a steam engine 1 . Sources (1) Atil et al., LLM Stability: A detailed analysis with some surprises ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

You were promoted Many skip the management steps In 9,830 Claude.ai conversations, 51.1 percent stated a goal, 15.8 percent questioned the reasoning and 8.7 percent checked facts; no study measures executing versus managing, so the research supports “many”, not “most” 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, The AI Fluency Index (February 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) academy.claude.com Workers describe the shift themselves In a survey of 319 weekly GenAI users, effort moved from executing tasks to stewarding them and from gathering information to verifying it, while higher confidence in the AI went with less checking 1 . Sources (1) Lee et al., The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers (CHI 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) microsoft.com Stepping stone: break it down Users split complex tasks into smaller steps, which creates a feedback loop where the model corrects course 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Economic Index: New building blocks for AI use (January 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Pocock's words are “communication barrier” He says there is a communication barrier between a person and an AI agent, located in vocabulary: they do not share the same language, so you need a shared language; the phrase “language barrier” is not his, and the management reading is this project's inference 1 . Sources (1) Matt Pocock, Software Fundamentals Matter More Than Ever (AI Engineer Europe 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) ai.engineer

Practise it today, at work Briefing, context and checking are the discipline Dell'Acqua 1 finds AI helps less experienced people on bounded tasks inside the model's competence; that effective delegation rests on briefing, supplying context and verifying is this project's inference from the research file, not a finding of the study. Sources (1) Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper 24-013, September 2023 (SSRN 4573321) ( opens in a new tab ) mitsloan.mit.edu A new AI session is a new contributor Experienced developers described AI as a new contributor lacking tacit knowledge of the repository, which is hard to hand over as context, and spent about 9 percent of their time reviewing and cleaning its output 1 . Sources (1) Becker, Rush, Barnes, Rein, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Experience with the tool predicts results Users with six months or more of tenure show a success rate about 3 to 5 points higher within the same task cluster and delegate less by directive; Anthropic notes learning by doing fits the data but is not proven 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning Curves (March 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Splitting tasks lengthens what you can finish Users split tasks into steps and pick tasks they expect to work, which accounts for part of the long task lengths seen in practice 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Economic Index: New building blocks for AI use (January 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

From execution to management 0:00 – 0:17 The question Imagine a colleague asks you over coffee: will AI reduce my work? Will it speed things up, so that by next year I do less? It is a fair question, and almost everybody starting out with AI asks it. 0:17 – 0:35 The reframe But the question rests on a faulty premise, because it assumes the tasks stay the same size. They don't. With AI you can now take on far more complex tasks than you could alone, and managing those tasks is the work AI adds. 0:35 – 0:52 The payoff So the better question is what you can now do. You accomplish much more, if you are willing to upskill and learn to manage AI like a team, and today is the chance to start moving in that direction.

Every revolution, one card 0:00 – 0:21 Every revolution, one card To see why, look at the three machines you already know: the plough, the steam engine and the computer. Each one took over the predictable work, the lifting, the digging, the calculating, and people moved to the part a machine could not do, which is judging, deciding and coordinating. 0:21 – 0:42 The climb Now watch what happens under each card. The plough digs, so the farmer plans the harvest. The engine does the lifting, so the worker plans the line. Every time, the machine did more, and you moved up a level, which means the work did not disappear, it changed. 0:42 – 1:08 The fork, no judgment Here is where it forks, and I want to say it without judgment. Picture two people in the same plant on the same Monday, one still on the line and one at the control desk, and both are doing honest work. What matters for you is that a seismic shift opens that door, and whether you step through it is your call. 1:08 – 1:26 Now it thinks What is different now is that AI is the first tool that does part of the unpredictable work itself. It works in natural language, it reasons, it is creative, it brainstorms, so for the first time you are managing something that thinks. 1:26 – 1:47 Biggest step That is the biggest step on the wall, because one person can now do tasks that used to need a whole team. The fork under the AI card is still open, and this next part is my hypothesis: it opens again, for anyone who wants to step through it.

You were promoted 0:00 – 0:17 You were promoted So here is the way to read it. AI promotes you. You move from doing the work to managing the work, and the work doesn't shrink, it changes, so that you can do things that were out of reach before. 0:17 – 0:34 The misalignment That move has a gap, and it is the biggest misalignment people face today. Many of us still sit in the execution box, acting as if we do the work ourselves, when the new job is to manage it. 0:34 – 0:53 Four stepping stones The way across is four stepping stones: break it down, write clear goals, review, and delegate. Notice that none of these is a technical skill, you already know them from working with people, and each one makes you more confident with what comes back. 0:53 – 1:19 The barrier And there is a reason the gap is real. Picture asking the AI for "the usual report" and getting back something polished that answers a question you never asked. Nothing broke, it just had none of the words in your head. So before your next handoff, spend one minute writing down the terms you take for granted, and use them every time.

Practise it today, at work 0:00 – 0:15 Practise on people The good news is that you don't have to wait for a new tool to practise this. You can practise on people, today, at work, so the people skills you already have become your AI skills. 0:15 – 0:35 The handoff Take the handoff. Next time you hand work to a colleague, before a vacation or any other time, give them a proper handoff with enough context to carry on without you. That is the same move as starting a new chat with the context in it. 0:35 – 0:49 The new teammate Or take the new teammate. When you onboard someone, treat it like opening a new AI session: nothing carries over unless you say it, so tell them what you would tell the AI. 0:49 – 1:11 Chunks and seams Then the big project. When you get a complex one, break it into smaller chunks and define the seams between them, so that each task contributes to the overall goal. Do that, and you can hand the chunks to people or to AI, and stay prolific without losing the thread. 1:11 – 1:27 An invitation Which brings it back to our coffee question. More complex projects are now within reach, which is not a burden, it is an invitation to grow, so which of these three rows will you start with this week?
